e_{5}=m_{1}m_{2}m_{3}m_{4}m_{5}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The leading coefficient is always \(1\), so \(k\ge 1\).

x^{5}=x^{5}-0x^{4}+0x^{3}-0x^{2}+0x-0,

Take the five distinct integers  

\[
m_{1}=-2,\qquad m_{2}=-1,\qquad m_{3}=0,\qquad m_{4}=1,\qquad m_{5}=2 .

Because the set is symmetric about \(0\),

\boxed{m_{1}=-2,\; m_{2}=-1,\; m_{3}=0,\; m_{4}=1,\; m_{5}=2},

\]

Now split the sum:

\[
S=\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n}}
   +\frac12\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n}}
      \Bigl(\frac{1}{(n-1)^{2}+1}
            +\frac{1}{(n+1)^{2}+1}\Bigr).
\]

\[

\[

\end{aligned}
\]

\cos6\theta&=\cos\frac{3\pi}{17}, &

\cos14\theta&=\cos\frac{7\pi}{17}, &
\cos16\theta&=\cos\frac{8\pi}{17}.
\end{aligned}

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^{8}(-1)^{k+1}\cos\frac{k\pi}{17}

### 1.  Reformulation

Give each unit square a value  
\[
c(v)=\begin{cases}
0 &\text{if the square is black},\\[2pt]
1 &\text{if the square is white}.
\end{cases}
\]

A *step* chooses an edge \(e=uv\) of the adjacency graph of the board and replaces  
\(c(u),c(v)\) by \(1-c(u),1-c(v)\); i.e. it adds the vector \(\mathbf 1_e\) (the
characteristic vector of the edge) to the colour vector, all calculations being
taken modulo \(2\).

Hence a sequence of steps changes the colour vector by the sum (mod 2) of the
chosen edges.  
If \(T\subseteq V\) is the set of squares that are white in the initial
colouring, the condition “all squares become black’’ is equivalent to finding
a set \(J\) of edges such that  

\[
\deg_J(v)\equiv
\begin{cases}
1 \pmod 2 & (v\in T),\\
0 \pmod 2 & (v\notin T),
\end{cases}\qquad (\ast)
\]

and the required number of steps is \(|J|\).  
Thus \(S(C)\) is the size of a *minimum \(T\)-join* in the \(8\times8\) grid,
where \(T\) is the set of initially white squares (its cardinality is even).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  An universal upper bound \(S(C)\le 32\)

Partition the board into the sixteen \(2\times2\) blocks  

\[
B_{ij}=\{(2i-1,2j-1),(2i-1,2j),(2i,2j-1),(2i,2j)\},
\qquad 1\le i,j\le4 .
\]

Inside a block there are at most four squares, and the number of white squares
in the block is even (the whole board has an even number of black squares,
hence also an even number of white squares in each block).  
For any even number of white squares in a \(2\times2\) block we can make them
all black using **at most two steps**:

* 0 white – nothing to do;
* 2 adjacent whites – flip the domino joining them (1 step);
* 2 diagonal whites – flip the two dominoes incident with one of the other
  squares (2 steps);
* 4 whites – flip the two dominoes of a perfect matching of the block (2
  steps).

Consequently each block needs at most two steps, and the whole board needs at
most  

\[
16\cdot 2 = 32\qquad\text{steps.}
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{S(C)\le 32\text{ for every initial colouring }C.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  A colouring that needs 32 steps

Consider the ordinary chessboard colouring: colour the squares of one
parity (say the “black’’ squares of a chessboard) white, and the other parity
black.  
There are \(32\) white squares, all lying on the same parity class of the
underlying checkerboard.

Observe that any domino (edge of the grid) always joins squares of opposite
parity.  Therefore **every edge can be incident to at most one of the white
squares**.  In a set \(J\) satisfying \((\ast)\) each white square must have
odd degree, i.e. at least one incident edge belonging to \(J\).  Because an
edge can serve at most one white square, we need at least as many edges as
white squares:

\[
|J|\ge |T| = 32 .
\]

Thus for this colouring \(S(C)\ge 32\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Optimality

The construction of Section 2 applied to the chessboard colouring attains
exactly \(32\) steps: each \(2\times2\) block contains two diagonal white
squares; the two dominoes described in the “2 diagonal whites’’ case give a
solution of size \(2\) per block, i.e. \(16\cdot2=32\) steps.  
Consequently  

\[
S(C)=32\quad\text{for this colouring}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Conclusion

All colourings satisfy \(S(C)\le 32\); the alternating (chessboard) colouring
requires exactly \(32\) steps.  Therefore the greatest possible value of
\(S(C)\) is

\[
\boxed{32}.
\]
